title: Typewriter and Regiment
premise: In 1917, Jude Marchetti serves as a battlefield nurse at a converted chateau field hospital, quietly keeping a private ledger of soldiers whose names officers have struck from official records to protect reputations. When an orphaned child is left at the hospital door with a note ordering everyone to forget his face, Jude recognizes the boy as the son of a colonel whose death was erased from the record—and realizes the ledger and the child are threads of the same cover-up. As a visiting inspector closes in and the workshop where the records are forged is slated for demolition, Jude must rally the found family of nurses, orderlies, and a disgraced clerk to finish restoring the erased names before the truth burns with the building. The novel ends with the ledger published, the boy claimed by an aunt who remembers his face, and Jude finally writing their own name on the last page.
about_author: Noor Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from the First World War. They write historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: POV Jude. At the Chateau Verrier field hospital, Jude triages the wounded while privately recording names that officers' reports omit—a shell-shocked private, a deserter executed without trial. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: Jude's sense that ink can hold what power wants to erase, and the loneliness of being the only one keeping count.

chapters.title: Instructions to Forget
chapters.summary: POV Jude. A boy of seven appears at the hospital door at dawn, clutching a note: forget his face. Matron wants him gone by transport; Jude hides him in the linen store. The beat is fear sharpening into protectiveness—Jude recognizes the boy's surname from a name in the ledger, the colonel reported 'missing, no dependents.'

chapters.title: The Workshop That Forges Absence
chapters.summary: POV Elias Quill, a disgraced army clerk assigned to the chateau's records workshop, where omissions are manufactured—death certificates rewritten, dependents struck. Elias glimpses Jude copying a page he himself destroyed weeks ago. The beat is guilt: he realizes the machinery of erasure has a human engine, and that Jude knows.

chapters.title: What Matron Carried Back From Ypres
chapters.summary: POV Matron Odile Ferrand, revealed through her memories as a nurse who once lost her own name to an administrative 'error.' She discovers the boy and, instead of reporting him, teaches Jude how records move through channels. The beat is reluctant alliance—found family forming around a shared wound.

chapters.title: An Inspector With Clean Gloves
chapters.summary: POV Jude. Major Aldous Renwick arrives to audit the hospital before its workshop is decommissioned and burned. He is charming, thorough, and asks oddly precise questions about the colonel's last week. Jude realizes the boy isn't just forgotten—he's being hunted. The beat is dread dressed in courtesy.

chapters.title: Names in the Margins
chapters.summary: POV Elias. Elias defects in the smallest way: he misfiles one document, then another, buying Jude time to cross-reference the ledger against workshop originals. The nurses form a silent relay. The beat is cautious hope—the first time the ledger has more than one keeper, and Jude feels less alone for it.

chapters.title: The Face They Were Told to Forget
chapters.summary: POV Jude. Renwick corners Jude with the boy's photograph and an offer: hand over the ledger, and the child goes to a 'better placement.' Jude refuses, and Renwick orders the workshop's demolition moved up to three days. The beat is open confrontation—power showing its face at last, and Jude's fear transmuting into resolve.

chapters.title: Three Days of Paper
chapters.summary: POV alternating Jude and Elias. The found family races to authenticate the ledger: a dying witness dictates testimony, Odile forges a chaplain's countersignature, Elias smuggles the original colonel's file out in a coffin's paperwork. The beat is desperate, tender momentum—each small act of courage binding them tighter.

chapters.title: What the Fire Was Meant to Take
chapters.summary: POV Jude. Demolition day: Renwick arrives to burn the workshop early, but Odile has already alerted a war-correspondent journalist, who witnesses the attempt. Renwick's own forged omissions are read aloud from the ledger. The beat is the climax—truth spoken in the presence of the man who bought its silence, and his power collapsing.

chapters.title: The Last Page
chapters.summary: POV Jude. Weeks later: the ledger is submitted to the war office and excerpted in the press; the colonel's aunt arrives to claim the boy and remembers his face perfectly. The workshop stands, repurposed as a records office for the missing. Jude writes their own full name into the ledger's final line. The beat is belonging—at last, counted.
